status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings, stating 'They show by systematic experiments that retinal adaptation begins at the dimmest detectable backgrounds given the intrinsic noise of the rods' and 'They successfully compare their experiments to human psychophysical experiments: human behavioral threshold begins to increase for backgrounds near 0.01 R*/rod/s, similar to the backgrounds (∼0.02 R*/rod/s) at which macaque ganglion cell thresholds began to increase.' No concerns were raised about the validity of these core findings.

Reviewers affirm that 'Adaptation occurs rapidly at the level of AII Amacrine cells when as few as 1 or 2 photons are absorbed within a collection of several hundred rods,' which directly supports the claims about individual photon control of gain and mean-based (not variance-based) gain control mechanisms. No methodological or interpretive concerns were raised about these findings.

Reviewers specifically critique the presentation of these findings, noting 'Inhibitory synaptic inputs were small (how small?), …did not show obvious structure (what is meant by obvious structure?)' and recommend the authors 'give a clear, quantitative description of the results.' While not rejecting the findings, reviewers indicate the evidence presentation lacks precision and clarity needed for full evaluation.

Reviewers express concern about the multiple definitions and measures of gain used throughout the manuscript, asking 'Is it really necessary to use so many measures of gain?' and noting confusion about whether different gain measures are equivalent. They request clarification that 'gain changes in the circuit affect both signal and noise.' This indicates uncertainty about how to interpret the quantitative relationships presented, though not rejection of the underlying data.

Reviewers affirm that 'Adaptation occurs rapidly at the level of AII Amacrine cells,' directly supporting the claims about rapid gain changes with time constants of 0.3-0.5 seconds. No concerns were raised about the kinetics measurements or their interpretation.

Reviewers explicitly support these findings, stating the adaptation occurs 'when as few as 1 or 2 photons are absorbed within a collection of several hundred rods,' which directly affirms the claims about spatial integration over hundreds of rods. No methodological concerns were raised about the spatial transfer experiments.

Reviewers affirm that 'Adaptation occurs rapidly at the level of AII Amacrine cells,' supporting the localization claims. They also note the choice of On parasol ganglion cells 'could be better rationalized at the beginning of Results,' which is a presentation issue rather than a challenge to the validity of the pathway localization findings.

Reviewers request 'a succinct summary of relevant retinal circuitry in Introduction' with better explanation of signal transmission, but do not challenge the accuracy of the anatomical and functional descriptions of the rod bipolar pathway or parasol ganglion cell properties. This is a presentation request rather than a scientific concern.
